props.title: The Pope of Greenwich Village
props.initialSlug: Two cousins' heist spirals into NYC mob trouble

sections.content: **The Pope of Greenwich Village** (1984) stands as a gritty character study of Italian-American life in NYC, powered by explosive performances from Eric Roberts and Mickey Rourke at their raw, magnetic peaks. Like Mean Streets (1973) before it, it captures the desperate hustle of small-time crooks trying to make it big. Director Stuart Rosenberg (who helmed **Cool Hand Luke** (1967)) brings a stark authenticity to the Greenwich Village setting, making the neighborhood itself a character in this tale of cousins Charlie and Paulie's ill-fated heist scheme.

sections.content: The film belongs to a vital subset of 1980s New York crime dramas that explored ethnic neighborhood dynamics, alongside works like **Year of the Dragon** (1985) and **Once Upon a Time in America** (1984). What sets Pope apart is its laser focus on the desperation of working-class strivers - guys who aren't major gangsters but can't resist the allure of one big score. Roberts and Rourke create an electric dynamic that influenced later partnership-driven crime films like **Miller's Crossing** (1990).

Rosenberg's direction maintains a documentary-like immediacy while building profound emotional stakes. The film's infamous "thumb scene" remains one of the most visceral moments in 1980s cinema, rivaling the intensity of **The Deer Hunter** (1978) or **Raging Bull** (1980). Yet beneath the violence lies a mournful examination of loyalty, family bonds, and the price of ambition in America's urban crucible. SUBHEAD: New York's Changing Criminal Landscape

movies.slug: Harvey Keitel's raw portrayal of a corrupt NYC cop spiraling out of control

sections.content: The film captures a pivotal moment when old-school neighborhood crime structures were facing pressure from both law enforcement and changing demographics. Like **Prince of the City** (1981) and **Q&A** (1990), it documents the erosion of traditional ethnic enclaves and their criminal hierarchies. The authenticity of locations and supporting characters creates a time capsule of a vanishing New York, similar to what **After Hours** (1985) achieved in its darker comic vision.
